name: Heat protectant

lead: Heat protectants are sprays, serums and leave-in treatments applied before blow-drying or flat-ironing. They are marketed to reduce dryness, breakage and frizz so hair keeps its shine and smoothness through regular heat styling.

Descriptions say they coat the hair shaft with a film of silicones or polymers that slows heat transfer and limits moisture loss, while water and conditioning agents spread heat and smooth the cuticle. Many products list protection up to about 450 degrees F (232 degrees C), and some add bond-repair ingredients. No clinical studies were found, so claims rest on product and stylist descriptions.

paras: People spray or work the product through damp or dry hair before using a dryer, flat iron or curling iron, then style as usual. It is used every time heat is applied. Industry descriptions state the products lessen but do not eliminate damage, particularly at high temperatures.
No specific harms were identified in the reviewed material. Heavy use of hot tools can still leave hair dry and brittle, and product buildup is possible with layered styling products.

angle.text: Heat protectants are applied before dryers and irons to cushion hair from heat, so it keeps its shine and smoothness over time. They coat the strand with a film that slows heat transfer. Claims rest on product descriptions rather than trials.

lead: Heat protectants are hair-styling products, sold as sprays, serums, creams and leave-in treatments, that are applied before blow-drying, flat-ironing or curling so the hair takes less damage from the heat. The payoff for appearance is hair that stays smoother, shinier and less frizzy or broken after regular heat styling, which keeps sleek, curled or straightened styles looking better for longer [1][2].

Descriptions say they coat the hair shaft with a film that slows heat transfer and limits moisture loss, and many products list protection up to about 450 degrees F (232 degrees C), with some also adding conditioning or bond-repair ingredients [1]. Wikipedia's article on hair conditioner describes thermal protectants as film-forming polymers that shield hair from blow-dryers and styling irons that can exceed 200 degrees C, and notes that some polymer pretreatments were shown to reduce breakage during combing and limit heat damage to keratin [2].

Hair irons themselves are described as capable of severe damage with overuse [3]. Product descriptions say heat protectants lessen but do not eliminate that damage [1]. No clinical trials of heat-protectant products were found.
infobox: Protection up to about 450 degrees F (232 degrees C) [1]
Silicones such as dimethicone, polymers, hydrolyzed proteins, oils [1][2]

paras: Products are applied to hair before heat styling. Descriptions list water-based formulas that absorb heat, silicone or polymer films that act as a physical barrier, and conditioning agents that smooth the cuticle [1]. Newer products are described as combining heat shielding with repair claims, using peptides, bond-repairing complexes, plant proteins and oils [1].

Wikipedia's hair-conditioner article says leave-in conditioners are applied to wet or dry hair and not rinsed out, usually contain silicones or light polymers, and offer some thermal and UV protection. Silicones such as dimethicone form a thin film that fills cuticle gaps, reduces friction and adds shine, and cationic surfactants smooth the surface of damaged hair [2].

According to one reference, heat removes bound water from hair, and heating wet hair rapidly can produce steam that cracks the cuticle; at higher temperatures, roughly above 180 to 200 degrees C, keratin proteins are described as denaturing [1]. Wikipedia explains that straighteners break the hydrogen bonds in the hair's cortex, which can re-form with moisture, and that bleaching, dyeing, weathering and heat styling strip the cuticle's lipid coating [3][2].

Heated styling tools date to the 1870s, when French hairdresser Marcel Grateau introduced heated metal implements, and Isaac K. Shero patented the first hair straightener in 1909; ceramic and electric irons with adjustable heat followed later [3]. Heat protectants are described as emerging in the late twentieth century as heat styling tools became common, with KMS Control, launched in 1984, named as one of the first dedicated products [1].

Product descriptions say heat protectants reduce breakage, frizz and dullness, and work best alongside lower heat settings [1]. Wikipedia reports that some polymer pretreatments reduced breakage during combing and limited heat damage to keratin [2]. Independent clinical measurement of the benefit of commercial products has not been published.

timeline.event: Marcel Grateau introduces heated metal styling implements [3].
Isaac K. Shero patents the first hair straightener [3].
KMS Control is launched as an early dedicated heat-styling protection product (as described) [1].
